verdicts.why: To institute or set up something is plain description of an act; choosing it over 'set up' or 'found' says nothing about the speaker's attitude.
To bring something about is neutral; the sentences show it used equally for a good reputation and for strict notions, with no side taken by the word.
To found one thing on another is a plain structural relation with no approval or contempt built in.
To rouse a feeling is neutral as to which feeling; the sentences show it exciting concern, respect, gratitude and attention alike, so the word itself does not judge.
Acting as a stimulant is a physiological description with no attitude attached.
Evoking sexual feeling is the meaning, not an attitude; the word is a plain near-clinical term beside 'arouse' and carries neither leer nor disapproval.
A physics term for raising energy level; purely technical, no judgement possible.
Producing a magnetic field is a technical description with no attitude.
Under this gloss the word is a register label for language without contractions or colloquialisms, a plain classification; the 'formal and cold' of the manners sentences belongs to a different sense.
Represented in symbolic form is a technical description with no approval or dismissal in it.
Logically deductive is a neutral classification of a kind of reasoning.
A discipline's vocabulary is named without judgement; any strength in 'your language too strong' comes from the modifier, not the noun.
The cognitive faculty of language is a plain technical referent with no attitude in the word.
The lyrics of a song are named descriptively; the word takes no side about them.
To live in a place is plain fact; 'occupy' beside 'live in' or 'inhabit' differs in register, not in attitude.
Holding a position or role is described without approval or contempt for the holder.
Something being on one's mind is described neutrally; the sentences show it used for observation, praise and prudent ideas alike with no side taken.
Filling the whole of a space or a span of time is plain measurement, not judgement.

Military occupation is an unpleasant referent, but 'occupy' is the plain historian's word for it; the aggression sits in the act, and the word itself neither condemns like 'overrun' nor flatters like 'liberate'.
Bringing people together for a shared purpose is described without attitude; the sentences apply it as readily to unfeeling sisters as to Elizabeth and Jane.
Becoming one, as in marriage, is a plain description of joining; any warmth in the sentences comes from context, not from the verb.
Possessing qualities in combination is a neutral statement of co-occurrence; the praise in 'capacity, taste, and elegance united' is in the nouns, not the verb.
